summary: Provides a framework for applying GMPLS and the Path Computation Element architecture to wavelength switched optical networks, examining routing and wavelength assignment. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6163 explains what control systems need to know when choosing routes and wavelengths in optical networks. It describes network components, path constraints, and possible divisions of work between routing, wavelength assignment, GMPLS, and PCE.

questions: what is routing and wavelength assignment
how do gmpls and pce work together for optical networks
subtitle: A framework for routing and wavelength assignment in optical networks.

tldr.problem: Wavelength-switched optical networks have path constraints that ordinary packet routing does not capture, including wavelength continuity and device-specific switching limits.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC models optical links and devices, compares three ways to divide routing and wavelength assignment, and lists information GMPLS and PCE systems need.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework that prepares for protocol extensions. It does not define new protocol messages.

sections.title: Wavelength-Switched Optical Networks
sections.content:
A Wavelength Switched Optical Network (WSON) uses wavelength-division multiplexing, and switches signals according to their center wavelength. Its components can include optical links, transmitters and receivers, reconfigurable optical add/drop multiplexers (ROADMs), wavelength converters, and electro-optical devices.

Nodes may have asymmetric switching capabilities, and signals may need to meet compatibility constraints. A path must use available resources and, where there are no converters, maintain one wavelength across its links. The RFC provides a framework for applying GMPLS and the Path Computation Element architecture; optical impairments are outside its detailed scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Optical networks carry signals on different wavelengths and route them through switching devices. A control system must know which wavelengths and connections each device supports before it can select a path.

sections.title: Modeling Links and Optical Devices
sections.content:
The RFC models a switch using a connectivity matrix: each entry records whether a wavelength on an input port can reach an output port. It also records wavelength restrictions for each port. ROADMs have switched connectivity, while devices such as splitters and fixed optical add/drop multiplexers have fixed connectivity.

Transmitters may use a fixed wavelength or tune within a range. Regenerators have different capabilities: 1R amplifies or compensates a signal, 2R adds noise suppression or reshaping, and 3R also recovers timing and retimes the signal. Converters may change wavelength, but their available inputs, outputs, and current use can constrain a path.
sections.plainLanguage: The network model records which ports can connect and which wavelengths each port accepts. It also records whether devices can regenerate or convert a signal and what limits apply.

sections.title: Three Ways to Assign Routes and Wavelengths
sections.content:
Routing and Wavelength Assignment (RWA) selects both the links in an optical path and the wavelengths used along it. With full conversion at every node, wavelengths can be assigned hop by hop. Without converters, one wavelength must remain available along the entire path.

In combined RWA, one entity chooses both the route and wavelengths and needs detailed network information. In separated R and WA, one entity proposes paths and another assigns wavelengths. In routing with distributed wavelength assignment, the route is chosen first and signaling narrows the available wavelength set hop by hop; this needs less shared information but may have higher blocking under heavy load.
sections.plainLanguage: RWA chooses a route and the wavelengths used on it. One system can choose both, separate systems can divide the work, or routers can narrow the wavelength choices as signaling travels.

sections.title: Information Needed by GMPLS and PCE
sections.content:
GMPLS already has wavelength labels and signaling support for distributed assignment. The RFC says control systems also need information about link wavelength ranges, transmitter tuning ranges, switch connectivity, port restrictions, converter properties, and wavelength availability. Signal compatibility may require information about modulation, forward error correction, bitrate, and protocol identifier.

A PCE can compute optical paths, including batch or backup-path requests, but needs the corresponding network state and constraints. Signaling does not yet indicate that a node should regenerate a signal using a shared or reconfigurable regenerator pool.
sections.plainLanguage: Path computation needs current information about free wavelengths and the limits of each device. Some regeneration choices also need signaling support that the RFC says is not yet available.

sections.title: Security and Information Disclosure
sections.content:
The RFC does not require changes to the security models for OSPF-TE, RSVP-TE, or PCEP. However, meeting RWA needs with existing protocols may increase their load and make denial-of-service attacks more concerning.

RWA also requires sharing detailed information about network devices and capabilities. Operators may want to keep some of that information private, so the RFC says its protection should be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: More path-computation traffic may increase the load on control protocols. The extra network details shared for wavelength selection may also need protection.
